claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
The starting eutectic alloy has high room-temperature strength.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility or brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries generate local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage.
The proposed intervention is one optimized post-solidification annealing step under an inert atmosphere.
The annealing treatment will drive selective solute diffusion and segregation toward the lamellar interfaces.
Controlled annealing can alter lamellar-boundary chemistry without significantly coarsening the primary phases.
Solute segregation will form a thin, continuous, solute-enriched layer at the lamellar boundaries.
The solute-enriched interfacial layer will be softer and more compliant than the untreated lamellar boundary.
The compliant interfacial layer will facilitate dislocation transfer and smoother dislocation motion.
Improved dislocation transfer will reduce dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Reduced interfacial stress concentrations will suppress microcrack initiation during straining.
The annealed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature fracture elongation than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Excessive coarsening caused by annealing would compromise the proposed mechanical-property benefits.
Failure to produce a sufficiently compliant segregated interface would compromise the proposed benefits.
